newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Fairfax says News Corp up to no good.
newsitem.headline: Fairfax says News Corp up to no good.

text.p: The chairman of newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd, Sir Laurence Street, said that rival News Corp Ltd was responsible for constant speculation that the company's ownership structure was unstable.
Street said the speculation by News Ltd, the local arm of Rupert Murdoch's global media group, had regrettably been repeated by Communications Minister Senator Richard Alston.

"It (Fairfax) has survived a great deal over the last decade and I don't think that these present stirrings are anything more than an irritating campaign by a competitor to suggest that the state of the register is unstable," Street told ABC Radio.

Alston said on the weekend that it was possible the Fairfax papers could one day be owned by separate companies, leading to statements by Street and the company's largest shareholder, Conrad Black, on Tuesday that Fairfax would not be broken up.

"He (Alston) has repeated the unfounded rumour that was in the News Ltd publication and of course every time an unfounded rumour is repeated it tends to enlarge its effect in the public perception," Street said.
The key Fairfax publications are The Sydney Morning Herald, Melbourne's The Age, and Australian Financial Review daily newspapers.

Black, the owner of Canadian media group Hollinger Inc, has a controlling 25 percent stake in Fairfax held through his Telegraph Plc unit. He has repeatedly said he was not content with this holding as it did not provide secure control and has sought government approval to increase it.

Murdoch, with a stake of about five percent, and Australian businessmen Kerry Packer with about 14 percent have each expressed interest in gaining control of Fairfax, in particular the company's stranglehold on classified advertising in the Sydney and Melbourne markets.
